subject: physics_2
question_text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of a compound microscope and explain its working. Derive an expression for its magnification.

verification.note: From FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students (physics section), Ch.2 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments, printed pp.14-15 — Section C, 8 marks. The 1+1+1+1+1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. THIS IS THE ONE QUESTION IN THE CHAPTER THAT SAYS 'Draw a neat labelled diagram', so the two diagram steps carry 1 mark each; every other figure in this chapter is authored at 0 marks. UN-NUMBERED PART: the book prints an extra part c) after this answer, on ultraviolet light and magnification, with no question number of its own. It is folded into this card as a final step at ZERO marks, because it is not part of the 8-mark question the book numbers. TRANSCRIPTION: the printed description writes 'rock and pinion'; the correct name is rack and pinion, and it is written correctly here with the slip recorded in that step's why. Hand-checked physically: m = m₀ × mₑ with m₀ = −v₀/u and mₑ = 1 + D/fₑ gives m = −(v₀/u)(1 + D/fₑ); with the object close to F₀ so that u ≈ −f₀ and v₀ ≈ L, this becomes m = −(L/f₀)(1 + D/fₑ) for the image at the near point, and m ≈ −LD/(f₀fₑ) for the image at infinity. All four printed equations are correct.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Description
lines: A compound microscope has two converging
lenses on a common principal axis.
The lens near the object is the objective. It
has a small aperture and a small focal
length.
The lens near the eye is the eyepiece. It has
a larger aperture and a larger focal length.
Both are fitted at the ends of a metal tube.
A rack and pinion arrangement moves the
tube and so sets the distance of the object
from the objective.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name both lenses and give the aperture and focal length of each.
steps.why: The objective is made small and strong so that it can be brought very close to the object and still form a large real image; the eyepiece is made larger so that the whole of that image can be seen at once. The book prints the adjusting mechanism as 'rock and pinion'; the correct name is rack and pinion, a toothed bar driven by a small gear wheel.
common_mistakes: Giving the objective the larger focal length. The objective has the SMALLER focal length.
Saying the two lenses are of different types. Both are converging.

Drawing the first image erect. The objective always inverts.

steps.margin_note: Diagram mark. I₁G₁ acts as the object for the eyepiece. The emerging rays diverge, and the dashed backward extensions give the enlarged virtual final image IG.
steps.why: The image made by the objective becomes the object for the eyepiece, so the same two-ray construction is used a second time. The dashed lines say that the final image is virtual and lies on the same side as the eyepiece object.

steps.label: Working
lines: The object OJ is placed just outside the
principal focus F₀ of the objective, so its
real image forms on the other side.
This image I₁G₁ forms beyond 2F₀ and is
real, inverted and magnified.
I₁G₁ acts as the object for the eyepiece. The
eyepiece is moved so that I₁G₁ lies within
its focal length.
The eyepiece then forms the final image IG
at the near point. It is virtual, inverted
and magnified.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Both images described: real inverted magnified, then virtual inverted magnified.
steps.why: The instrument magnifies twice, once at each lens, which is why a compound microscope reaches far higher powers than a single magnifier. The final image is inverted because the objective inverts once and the eyepiece does not invert again.
common_mistakes: Calling the final image real. It is virtual — the eyepiece is used as a magnifier.
Saying the final image is erect. It is inverted with respect to the object.

recall.must_convey: That the objective forms a real inverted magnified image beyond 2F₀, which acts as the object for the eyepiece, and the eyepiece forms a virtual inverted magnified final image at the near point.

steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. State the product rule and give m₀ with its minus sign.
steps.why: The second lens magnifies whatever the first one hands to it, so the two factors multiply rather than add. The minus sign in m₀ records that the objective inverts the image.

Dropping the minus sign in m₀, which loses the inversion.

steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Name the eyepiece as a simple microscope — that is where 1 + D/fₑ comes from.
steps.why: Nothing new has to be derived for the eyepiece, because it is used exactly as a magnifier: an object inside its focal length, an eye at the far side, and a virtual image at the near point. The simple-microscope result therefore carries over unchanged.
common_mistakes: Writing mₑ = D/fₑ for the near-point case. That form belongs to the image at infinity.
Using f₀ in place of fₑ in the bracket.

steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Both approximations stated: u ≈ −f₀ and v₀ ≈ L.
steps.why: These two approximations replace the two quantities that change while the instrument is focused by two fixed lengths of the instrument itself. The result is a formula in f₀, fₑ, L and D alone, all of which are known once the microscope is built.

Leaving L undefined. L is the distance between the two lenses.

steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. Give the infinity form and say what the minus sign means.
steps.why: With both focal lengths in the denominator, a microscope is made powerful by making both lenses short-focus. The image at infinity is the setting a user chooses for long viewing, because the eye stays relaxed.
common_mistakes: Writing m ≈ −LD/(f₀ + fₑ). The two focal lengths MULTIPLY in the denominator.
Ignoring the minus sign, which is what records the inversion.

steps.memory_tip: Both focal lengths sit below the line, so short lenses give a strong microscope.

steps.label: Ultraviolet light
lines: Ultraviolet light has a smaller wavelength
than visible light, so a lens used with it
has a smaller focal length.
A smaller focal length gives a larger
magnification, so the magnification
increases when ultraviolet light is used.
steps.margin_note: The book prints this extra part with no question number of its own. It carries no marks here; write it only if the paper asks for it.
steps.why: The focal length of a lens depends on the refractive index of its material, and the refractive index is larger for shorter wavelengths. Ultraviolet light therefore sees a shorter-focus lens than visible light does, and since m ∝ 1/f the magnification rises. This is the reason ultraviolet microscopes resolve finer detail than visible-light ones.
common_mistakes: Saying the magnification falls. A smaller focal length gives a LARGER magnification.
Explaining it by the brightness of the light. The reason is the focal length, through the wavelength.

recall.must_convey: That ultraviolet light has a smaller wavelength, so the focal length is smaller, and since m ∝ 1/f the magnification increases.
accept: ultraviolet has a smaller wavelength so the focal length is smaller
m is proportional to one by f so the magnification increases

reject: m is about minus L D by f nought f e

steps.memory_tip: Shorter wave, shorter focus, bigger magnification — three steps in one line.

insider_note: Two diagrams and four equations. The chain is short: multiply the two magnifications, then replace u by f₀ and v₀ by L.
